questions.stem: A highly toxic powder is released from one charging port directly beside the operator. Which ventilation strategy is most appropriate?
options: Enclose the charging point and capture the powder with local exhaust before it enters the breathing zone.
Use general comfort ventilation to mix the powder uniformly through the room.
Increase room temperature so buoyancy carries all particles away from the worker.
Install a high-velocity supply fan behind the operator and rely on it to carry the powder across the room.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Local exhaust is preferred for high-hazard contaminants and point sources because it captures emissions near their origin before they disperse through the room.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Diluting a highly toxic point-source particulate exposes more of the room and may require impractical airflow.
Heating does not provide controlled source capture and may change dispersion unpredictably.
A supply jet can drive the contaminant through the breathing zone unless source-worker-hood geometry is controlled.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 3 — Ventilation Investigation
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 9, ventilation selection and local exhaust, pp. 294-305; OSHA OTM Section III, Chapter 3, dilution versus local exhaust

questions.stem: Which condition most strongly supports considering dilution ventilation as an exposure control?
options: A highly toxic dust is projected from a single grinder toward the worker.
A moderate-toxicity vapor is generated uniformly from distributed sources with adequate mixing and make-up air.
An upset can release an unknown, rapidly varying vapor quantity, but the room has a high-capacity general exhaust fan.
A dense particulate is released from a single machine and must be transported through ducts without settling.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Dilution can be suitable for gases or vapors of moderate toxicity when generation is predictable, sources are dispersed, mixing is adequate, and required air volumes are feasible.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A high-hazard particulate point source calls for source enclosure and local exhaust.
Unknown or rapidly varying generation makes a dilution design unreliable for controlling peaks.
Particulate transport and source capture are local-exhaust design concerns, not a good dilution application.

questions.stem: Air velocity is 1,600 ft/min in an 18-in.-diameter round duct. What is the approximate volumetric airflow?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The diameter is 1.5 ft, so area = π(0.75 ft)² = 1.767 ft². Q = VA = 1,600 × 1.767 ≈ 2,827 cfm, or about 2,830 cfm.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This multiplies velocity by the radius rather than by cross-sectional area.
This multiplies by the diameter in inches instead of converting and calculating area.
This is approximately twice the correct flow and results from an incorrect circular area.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 3 — Ventilation Investigation
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 9, volumetric airflow, pp. 296-297; OSHA OTM ventilation primer

incorrectOptionExplanations: This multiplies 4,005 directly by 0.36 instead of by its square root.
This divides by √0.36 instead of multiplying.
This applies an additional factor to the velocity-pressure relationship.

questions.stem: At a point upstream of an exhaust fan, static pressure is −1.8 in. water gauge and velocity pressure is 0.5 in. water gauge. What is total pressure at that point?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Total pressure is the algebraic sum: TP = SP + VP = −1.8 + 0.5 = −1.3 in. water gauge.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This subtracts velocity pressure instead of adding it algebraically.
This ignores the negative static-pressure sign upstream of the fan.
This adds magnitudes and also changes the sign.

incorrectOptionExplanations: This omits the conversion from minutes to hours.
This uses an incorrect room volume or airflow ratio.
This introduces a factor-of-ten error.

questions.stem: Contaminant generation has stopped in a 40,000-ft³ room. The effective ventilation rate is 2,000 cfm. Assuming complete mixing, how long will it take to reduce concentration from 300 ppm to 30 ppm?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This calculates V/Q′, the time constant, but does not apply the logarithmic concentration ratio.
This treats a tenfold concentration reduction as a ten-minute arithmetic change.
This doubles the correct logarithmic purge time.

questions.stem: A vapor is generated at 0.8 ft³/min and the effective dilution airflow is 4,000 cfm. Assuming steady state and complete expression of the ratio as ppm, what concentration is expected?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: C = G/Q′ = 0.8/4,000 = 0.0002 by volume. Multiplying by 10⁶ gives 200 ppm.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This reports the volume fraction as though it were already ppm.
This reverses the generation-to-airflow ratio.
This uses an unrelated multiplication of generation and airflow.

incorrectOptionExplanations: This omits the mixing factor of 3.
This applies the mixing factor twice.
This introduces a factor-of-ten error in evaporation rate or unit conversion.

questions.stem: Hot vapors rise from a heated tank, and the operator can remain outside the upward contaminant path. Which hood type is most appropriate among the listed choices?
options: A downdraft table that pulls the plume through the worker’s upper body.
A canopy hood positioned above the tank to receive the rising thermal plume.
A plain opening placed far from the tank with no enclosure or capture analysis.
A general supply diffuser directed across the tank toward the operator.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A canopy hood can receive hot gases or vapors that rise naturally, provided the worker is not positioned between the source and the hood and cross-drafts are controlled.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This arrangement could draw rising vapors through the breathing zone and opposes the plume direction.
Capture falls rapidly with distance, so a remote opening may be ineffective.
The supply jet can spread the contaminant and disrupt capture.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 3 — Ventilation Investigation
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 9, canopy, downdraft, enclosure, and receiving hoods, pp. 305-306; OSHA OTM hood selection

questions.concept: Capture velocity at a plain opening
questions.stem: A plain-opening hood moves 900 cfm. The source is 1.0 ft from the opening, and the hood area is 0.75 ft². Using V = Q/(10X² + A), what is the approximate capture velocity at the source?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides flow by hood area and ignores distance from the opening.
This introduces an extra factor of ten in the denominator.
This calculates face velocity Q/A rather than capture velocity at the remote source.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 3 — Ventilation Investigation

questions.stem: A local exhaust hood has the specified flow, but a pedestal fan pushes the contaminant plume past the operator before it reaches the hood. What is the best corrective action?
options: Increase the fan speed at the pedestal fan to move the plume faster.
Verify only the design duct velocity and accept the hood even though the plume crosses the worker’s breathing zone.
Rely on respirators and leave the conflicting airflows unchanged.
Remove or redirect the cross-draft and reposition the source, worker, and hood so the plume enters the hood first.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Total airflow alone does not prove effective capture. Cross-drafts and poor geometry can overpower hood-induced velocity and carry contaminant through the worker’s breathing zone.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A stronger cross-draft can further defeat local capture.
Duct flow does not confirm that contaminant is captured at the source.
Respirators may be needed temporarily, but the engineering-control defect should be corrected.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 3 — Ventilation Investigation
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 9, local exhaust and capture velocity, pp. 305-310; OSHA OTM Section III, Chapter 3, hood and cross-draft evaluation

questions.stem: Which instrument arrangement is used to determine velocity pressure inside a ventilation duct?
options: A Pitot tube connected to a differential-pressure instrument.
A smoke tube used as the sole quantitative pressure instrument.
A noise dosimeter attached to the duct wall.
A sorbent tube connected directly to a manometer.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A Pitot traverse measures pressure components in the duct. Velocity pressure can then be converted to air velocity using the applicable relationship and density correction.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Smoke visualizes airflow direction and capture but does not provide a quantitative velocity-pressure reading.
A dosimeter integrates sound exposure and does not measure ventilation pressure.
A sorbent tube collects contaminants; it is not a pressure probe.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 3 — Ventilation Investigation
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 9, ventilation measurement equipment and Pitot tubes, p. 312; OSHA OTM ventilation primer

questions.stem: After a large exhaust fan is commissioned, exterior doors become difficult to open and measured hood flows fall below design. What is the most likely system issue?
options: The room has too much make-up air, which always lowers exhaust flow.
Insufficient make-up air is causing excessive negative pressure and reduced exhaust flow.
The hoods are necessarily oversized because doors are hard to open.
Increase fan speed immediately without evaluating replacement air, room pressure, or the supply-air system.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Air removed by exhaust must be replaced. Inadequate make-up air increases building negative pressure, can reduce fan delivery, disrupt hood capture, and draw uncontrolled air through openings.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The described door pressure and reduced hood flow are characteristic of insufficient replacement air.
Hood size alone does not explain whole-building negative pressure after a major exhaust increase.
Increasing exhaust without adequate replacement air can worsen the pressure imbalance.
